question: Explain Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and why it forms the foundation for hypothesis testing and confidence intervals.
idealAnswer: The Central Limit Theorem states that the distribution of sample means approaches a normal Gaussian distribution as sample size N increases (typically N >= 30), regardless of the shape of the underlying population distribution.

question: Explain Parametric vs Non-Parametric statistical tests (t-test, ANOVA vs Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis).
idealAnswer: Parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA) assume data follows a specific distribution (normal) and test parameters like mean and variance. Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon) make no distribution assumptions and evaluate ranks/medians for skewed data.
ideal_answer: Parametric tests (t-test, ANOVA) assume data follows a specific distribution (normal) and test parameters like mean and variance. Non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, Wilcoxon) make no distribution assumptions and evaluate ranks/medians for skewed data.
explanation: Evaluates Data Science Statistical Testing and Parametric vs Non-Parametric Tests comprehension.

question: What is the Curse of Dimensionality in data science, and how does it degrade distance metrics and model convergence?
idealAnswer: As feature dimensions increase, volume of space grows exponentially, making data points extremely sparse. In high-dimensional space, Euclidean distances between all pairs of points become nearly identical, degrading distance-based algorithms (KNN, K-Means) and increasing overfitting risks.

question: Explain Feature Importance vs SHAP Values vs Permutation Importance for machine learning model interpretability.
concept: Feature Importance vs Permutation vs SHAP
idealAnswer: MDI (tree impurity reduction) is biased toward high-cardinality features. Permutation Importance measures score drop when a feature column is randomly shuffled (model-agnostic). SHAP values calculate game-theoretic marginal contributions per feature with direction and magnitude.

question: How do you handle Multicollinearity in regression models: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), Correlation Matrix, and PCA?
idealAnswer: Multicollinearity occurs when independent features are highly correlated, inflating standard errors and making regression coefficients unstable. Detected using Variance Inflation Factor: VIF > 5-10 indicates severe multicollinearity; resolved by dropping redundant features or applying PCA/Ridge regression.

question: Explain Survival Analysis: Kaplan-Meier Estimator, Censored Data (Right Censoring), and Cox Proportional Hazards Model.
idealAnswer: Survival analysis models time until an event occurs (churn, equipment failure). It handles Censored Data (when the event is unobserved during study duration). Kaplan-Meier estimates survival curves over time. Cox Proportional Hazards evaluates how covariates influence hazard rates.

question: What is Causal Inference: Confounders, Propensity Score Matching (PSM), Difference-in-Differences (DiD), and Instrumental Variables?
idealAnswer: Correlation does not imply causation. Causal inference estimates true treatment effects from observational data: Propensity Score Matching (PSM) balances treated and control groups on confounding covariates. Difference-in-Differences (DiD) compares pre/post changes between groups.
ideal_answer: Correlation does not imply causation. Causal inference estimates true treatment effects from observational data: Propensity Score Matching (PSM) balances treated and control groups on confounding covariates. Difference-in-Differences (DiD) compares pre/post changes between groups.
explanation: Evaluates Data Science Causal Inference and Causal Inference & Propensity Score Matching comprehension.

question: Explain Time Series Forecasting models: ARIMA (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average), SARIMA (Seasonal), and Prophet.
idealAnswer: ARIMA models non-seasonal stationary time series with (p, d, q) parameters: Autoregression (p), Differencing (d) for stationarity, and Moving Average (q). SARIMA adds seasonal parameters (P, D, Q, s). Prophet handles non-linear trends, multiple seasonalities, and holiday effects using decomposable additive curves.
ideal_answer: ARIMA models non-seasonal stationary time series with (p, d, q) parameters: Autoregression (p), Differencing (d) for stationarity, and Moving Average (q). SARIMA adds seasonal parameters (P, D, Q, s). Prophet handles non-linear trends, multiple seasonalities, and holiday effects using decomposable additive curves.
explanation: Evaluates Data Science Time Series Forecasting and ARIMA, SARIMA, & Facebook Prophet comprehension.

question: How do you test for Stationarity in Time Series data: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) Test, KPSS Test, and Differencing?
idealAnswer: Stationary series have constant mean and variance over time. Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests for a unit root (p-value < 0.05 rejects null hypothesis, confirming stationarity). KPSS tests the null hypothesis of stationarity. Non-stationary data is made stationary via log transforms and differencing.
ideal_answer: Stationary series have constant mean and variance over time. Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests for a unit root (p-value < 0.05 rejects null hypothesis, confirming stationarity). KPSS tests the null hypothesis of stationarity. Non-stationary data is made stationary via log transforms and differencing.
explanation: Evaluates Data Science Time Series Diagnostics and Stationarity Testing (ADF & KPSS) comprehension.

question: Explain Recommendation Systems: Collaborative Filtering (User-User, Item-Item), Matrix Factorization (SVD / ALS), and Content-Based Filtering.
idealAnswer: Content-based filtering recommends items similar to previously liked items. Collaborative filtering recommends items based on user similarity matrices. Matrix Factorization (SVD/ALS) decomposes user-item interaction matrices into low-rank latent user and item factor vectors.
ideal_answer: Content-based filtering recommends items similar to previously liked items. Collaborative filtering recommends items based on user similarity matrices. Matrix Factorization (SVD/ALS) decomposes user-item interaction matrices into low-rank latent user and item factor vectors.

question: What is the Cold-Start Problem in Recommendation Systems, and how do hybrid recommender models solve it for new users/items?
idealAnswer: The cold-start problem occurs when new users or items have zero historical interaction data, breaking collaborative filtering. Solved by falling back to content-based metadata features, popularity-ranked items, demographic profiling, or active onboarding preference questionnaires.
ideal_answer: The cold-start problem occurs when new users or items have zero historical interaction data, breaking collaborative filtering. Solved by falling back to content-based metadata features, popularity-ranked items, demographic profiling, or active onboarding preference questionnaires.

question: Explain Anomaly Detection techniques: Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor (LOF), and Autoencoders.
idealAnswer: Isolation Forest isolates anomalies in decision trees with few random feature splits (anomalies have short path lengths). One-Class SVM learns a hypersphere boundary enclosing normal data. Autoencoders flag anomalies with high reconstruction error.

question: Explain Resampling and Bootstrap: Monte Carlo Simulations, Bootstrapping Confidence Intervals, and Permutation Tests.
